summary: Single deployable monolith: Go (net/http + chi), PostgreSQL (managed or self-hosted) database on Google Cloud Run. It keeps data in US regions, matches the team's languages and is estimated at $230-$390 per month.

architecture.name: monolith
architecture.justification: One deployable is the fastest to build and simplest to run for a team of 3 and 2 feature areas (payments, multi-tenancy).

alternatives.why_not: Adds service boundaries, network calls and per-service deployment that this team does not need at this scale (team 3).
With 2 feature areas the code base stays small enough that formal module boundaries mostly add ceremony; adopt them once a third feature area arrives.
Per-request functions suit light, spiky work; this backend runs as a long-lived service on Google Cloud Run, which suits websockets, background jobs and steady traffic better.

frontend.justification: No client application is built because the project is API-only.

alternatives.why_not: Every other frontend option fails a hard constraint for this scenario.

backend.justification: Go (net/http + chi) matches the team's go skills; compiled, low latency; is a proven choice for api platform projects.

alternatives.why_not: C# + ASP.NET Core scores 3.3 points lower overall, mainly on team skill fit (2.6 points) and compatibility with the rest of the stack (0.6 points).
Java + Spring Boot scores 3.6 points lower overall, mainly on team skill fit (2.6 points) and cost (0.6 points).

tradeoffs: No batteries, more code per feature

database.choice: Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL in Iowa (us-central1)
database.justification: PostgreSQL gives ACID transactions for money-handling data; can be placed in Iowa (us-central1) to keep data in the US; excellent query planner, rich indexing. It runs as Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, the managed service on the same cloud as the application, so backups, patching and failover are the provider's job.

alternatives.why_not: MySQL (managed or self-hosted) scores 1.8 points lower overall, mainly on coverage of the required features (0.7 points) and security (0.5 points).

CockroachDB scores 2.6 points lower overall, mainly on cost (0.5 points) and compatibility with the rest of the stack (0.5 points). Estimated infrastructure about $130-$280/month versus about $190-$350/month.

tradeoffs: Write scaling beyond one primary needs design

hosting.justification: Google Cloud Run runs on GCP as preferred; can be placed in Iowa (us-central1) to keep data in the US; offers a 99.95% SLA, in line with the 99.95% target; cold starts, request concurrency.

alternatives.why_not: Google Compute Engine scores 2.1 points lower overall, mainly on maintainability (0.7 points) and time to market (0.5 points).
Firebase Hosting scores 12.4 points lower overall, mainly on vendor lock-in (3.9 points) and team skill fit (2.6 points).

supporting.justification: Google Cloud Identity Platform: users sign in (email password); Firebase Authentication with an SLA, multi-tenancy and HIPAA coverage; free at this scale.

alternatives.why_not: A close second with a smaller fit to this stack; score 0.84 vs 0.85.
Ranks lower (costs more (about $30 vs $0 per month at the high end)); score 0.78 vs 0.85.

tradeoffs: Priced per monthly active user past the free tier; GCP-specific setup

supporting.justification: Stripe: the product takes payments; best developer experience and global coverage; free at this scale.

alternatives.why_not: Ranks lower (lower quality rating (9 vs 10)); score 0.82 vs 0.86.
Ranks lower (lower quality rating (7 vs 10)); score 0.63 vs 0.86.

tradeoffs: Per-transaction fees; payouts and some methods vary by country

supporting.justification: Google Cloud API Gateway: a public API product needs keys, per-customer rate limits and usage metering; managed gateway in front of Cloud Run with API keys and quotas.

alternatives.why_not: Ranks lower (more to operate); score 0.75 vs 0.77.

tradeoffs: Fewer policies than Apigee; per-customer billing still needs your own metering export

supporting.justification: Postmark: email and password sign-in needs verification and reset emails; high deliverability for transactional email.

alternatives.why_not: Ranks lower (lower quality rating (8 vs 9)); score 0.80 vs 0.83.
Ranks lower (lower quality rating (8 vs 9)); score 0.79 vs 0.83.

tradeoffs: Transactional email only; marketing email needs a separate stream

supporting.justification: GitHub Actions: automated build and deploy for the team; workflows next to the code; the 2,000 free minutes a month cover a small team, larger teams buy extra minutes; free at this scale.

alternatives.why_not: Ranks lower (lower quality rating (8 vs 9), costs more (about $25 vs $0 per month at the high end), more to operate); score 0.77 vs 0.84.
Ranks lower (lower quality rating (7 vs 9), more to operate); score 0.56 vs 0.84.

tradeoffs: Minute limits on private repositories; long builds need paid or self-hosted runners

supporting.justification: Sentry: production monitoring for the availability target; error tracking and performance with free developer plan.

alternatives.why_not: Ranks lower (lower quality rating (8 vs 9), more to operate); score 0.78 vs 0.82.
Ranks lower (lower quality rating (8 vs 9), more to operate); score 0.76 vs 0.82.

tradeoffs: Event quota per plan; sample high-volume errors

assumptions: Load estimate: peak about 40 requests/second and about 12M requests/month from 3K users in 12 months.
Usage-priced items are shown as a band (0.75x to 1.3x of the estimate) because load figures are order-of-magnitude.
Public list prices of each product, in USD, without taxes, committed-use discounts or developer time.
The 99.95% availability target doubles or adds redundancy for hosting and database where needed.
API gateway (Google Cloud API Gateway): about $27-$35/month

warnings.message: Use a hosted checkout from a PCI DSS certified provider so card data never reaches your servers.

SOC 2 audits your own controls (access reviews, change management, logging, incident response); vendors with their own SOC 2 report shorten the audit, and gaps in the chosen stack are listed separately.

assumptions: No extra inputs supplied; neutral defaults are used (learning appetite medium, lock-in tolerance medium, budget strictness firm, no hiring plan, no mobile preference).
No cache layer: about 40 requests/second and 3,000 users in 12 months are served directly by the database or BaaS.
No queue: background work is light enough for the backend or the provider's own webhooks and functions.
